title: Anatomy of a Policy Decision
subtitle: PEP, PDP, PIP, PAP — the XACML boxes that actually matter
content:
🧱 The Four Boxes (XACML vocabulary, universal idea)

  • PEP — Policy Enforcement Point: intercepts the request (sidecar, gateway filter, middleware). Asks, then enforces. Never decides.
  • PDP — Policy Decision Point: evaluates policy + attributes, returns ALLOW/DENY (+ reason). OPA, Cedar engine, OpenFGA server, PlainID PDP.
  • PIP — Policy Information Point: supplies attributes (groups, clearance, time, device posture). HR system, IdP, device inventory.
  • PAP — Policy Administration Point: authors, versions, ships policy (Git + bundle pipeline + Immuta/PlainID consoles).

🔁 The Decision Lifecycle

  1. Client calls GET /reports/q3 with a JWT.
  2. PEP intercepts, extracts subject/action/resource/context.
  3. PEP queries PDP: may S do A on R given C?
  4. PDP loads the current policy bundle; pulls attributes from PIPs.
  5. PDP evaluates: default DENY unless a permit rule matches (and no forbid overrides).
  6. PDP returns decision + determining policy ids (audit trail).
  7. PEP enforces: forward or 403. Every denial is logged with its reason.

📨 What Travels in an AuthZ Query

Subject (who: id, roles, groups, tenant), action (what verb: read/write/delete, preferably resource:action), resource (which object: type, id, owner, tenant, labels), context (when/where/how: time, IP, MFA, device). If any of the four is missing, the policy cannot decide correctly — schema it.

⚠️ Two Classic Confusions

  • PEP vs PDP: putting rule logic in the middleware is the scattered-if-statement problem. The PEP maps routes to permission strings; the PDP owns the rules.
  • AuthN tokens vs AuthZ attributes: a JWT proves identity and carries claims, but group membership, clearance, and resource labels usually come from PIPs at decision time — fresher than token issuance.

questions.question: A sidecar intercepts GET /payments/123, asks the engine, then forwards or returns 403. Which box is the sidecar?

options.text: PEP — it intercepts and enforces, but does not decide
PDP — it makes the allow/deny decision
PAP — it authors and versions policy

questions.explanation: Enforcement (intercept + forward/deny) is the PEP job. The decision comes from the PDP. Mixing them recreates scattered authorization logic.

questions.question: Which component returns ALLOW/DENY for (subject, action, resource, context)?

options.text: PDP — the policy decision point (OPA, Cedar engine, OpenFGA, PlainID PDP)

questions.explanation: The PDP owns evaluation. Everything else feeds it (PIP), asks it (PEP), or ships to it (PAP).

questions.question: Group membership, clearance level, and device posture arrive at decision time from HR/IdP/device systems. What are these systems?

options.text: PIPs — policy information points supplying attributes

questions.explanation: Attributes flow from PIPs. Freshness matters: group changes should affect decisions without waiting for token re-issue.

questions.question: An authZ query contains subject + action but no resource identifier. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: Policy cannot check ownership or tenancy — decisions become coarse allow/deny for whole APIs

questions.explanation: BOLA lives here. Without the resource (type, id, owner, tenant), the PDP can only answer role-wide questions, never is-this-subject-allowed-this-object.

questions.question: Where should the rule 'analysts may read only their own tenant' live?

options.text: In PDP policy, with the PEP only mapping the route to a permission string

questions.explanation: PEP maps (route → permission/action); PDP owns rules. That split keeps one auditable source of truth and lets tests cover the invariant once.

questions.question: A user's department changes in HR but decisions use yesterday's value. Which box is stale?

options.text: PIP feed (attribute freshness) — shorten sync or read through at decision time

questions.explanation: Decisions are only as fresh as their attributes. PIP latency is an authorization parameter, not an HR detail.

questions.question: A request arrives with subject and resource but no action. What should the PDP do?

options.text: Deny — an action-less query cannot match least-privilege rules; fix the PEP to send it
Guess read, since reads are safe
Ask the end user what they meant

questions.explanation: Every AuthZ query needs all four elements. Guessing the verb is how write-access hides inside read-shaped holes.

questions.question: Two services ask the same PDP the same question and get different answers. First suspect?

options.text: They sent different inputs — stale attributes or different resource ids

questions.explanation: PDPs are deterministic over (policy, input). Divergent answers mean divergent inputs — diff them before blaming the engine.
